F1.Q1: Dry-laid stone paving — large tan-grey flags, irregular sizes, mortared. That's as far as I can honestly take it. I can tell you it's *stone slabs*; I cannot tell you what kind of stone, whether it's cut or salvaged, or whether it's the same stone as the last room.
F1.Q1_WHY:
The read comes entirely from the *joint layout*, not the material. Across x 185–630, y 0–395 there's a continuous mesh of running-bond-ish rectangles of varying size (a 90×30px slab at x 470–553 y 50–79, a 70×30 at x 205–275 y 300–330, small 25×20 units at x 555–615 y 130–200). Rectangular units of mixed size, staggered, with mortar between = paving. The faces themselves are flat tonal fill; they carry no grain, no bedding, no aggregate, no colour variation between one slab and its neighbour beyond a couple of degrees of tint. I'm reading the *diagram* of a stone floor and inferring the stone.

---
F1.Q2:
South, into the corridor mouth at x 376–433, y 395+.

Nothing about the ground influenced that. I picked it because it's a two-tile gap in a wall and it's near the figure. I checked the ground at that mouth (x 376–433, y 370–395) against the ground at the west mouth (x 183–210, y 205–275) and against open floor nowhere near either (x 280–330, y 220–260) — the joint pattern, tone and surface treatment are indistinguishable. I routed by the negative space in the walls. That is a random choice dressed up as a decision.

---
F1.Q3: It's been cracked and nothing else. Long fracture lines run across it; the stones themselves are untouched. No spalling at the crack lips, no lifted or dropped slabs, nothing spilled, nothing dragged, nothing burnt, nothing patched, nothing repaired. For a place in continuous heavy use since before the records, the floor has no history on it — it has one event, drawn once.
F1.Q3_WHY:
The cracks are the only damage vocabulary present. Trace the main one: it enters at x≈355 y≈35, runs down to x≈350 y≈250, then splays into three branches heading southeast through x 400 y 300 → x 490 y 330 → x 630 y 370. A second runs from x≈185 y≈215 east to x≈300 y≈250. They are 1px near-black polylines and they cross slab joints *mid-face without any change* — at x 353 y 150 the crack passes straight through a joint and the joint neither offsets it nor interrupts it. Real fracture propagates along mortar or steps at it. This one is drawn over the top of the tile grid as a separate layer. Contrast at the lamp is stark (crack luminance 52 against floor 144 at y 150, x 353); out at y 330 x 269 it's 19 against 27, so it's correctly lit — but it's still a line on a surface, not a break in one.

---
F1.Q4:
Yes — two things.

**One: the 45° hatch.** A short dotted diagonal stroke, lower-left to upper-right, sitting near the middle of the slab face. It is on nearly every large slab in the room and it is *always the same angle, same 1px dotted construction, same length band*. Count them in one crop, x 400–560 / y 20–200: I count it on the slab at x 470–553 y 50–79, on x 483–520 y 85–115, on x 520–560 y 85–115, on x 415–465 y 155–185, on x 500–555 y 155–190. Same crop, five slabs, five identical strokes. It repeats again out west: x 215–260 y 30–60, x 270–320 y 45–75, x 250–300 y 250–285. It is one stamp applied everywhere and once you see it you cannot stop counting it.

**Two: the vertical tally.** Three-to-five short vertical ticks in a row, in the same relative position on the slab. At x 555–580 y 132–158, x 585–612 y 132–158, x 505–535 y 175–200, x 235–265 y 305–330. Same motif, same spacing.

Both pull attention off the scene and onto the texture pipeline.

---
F1.Q5:
**Repeated.** Not tiled — the joint *layout* is genuinely varied and non-periodic (I autocorrelated the floor region after removing the lighting gradient; peak correlation across periods 6–90px is only 0.195 at 24px, so there's no hard tile stamp in the geometry). The repetition is in the *decoration*. Faces get one of about three stamps — blank, 45° hatch, vertical tally — dropped in the same relative position at the same scale and the same angle. A near-duplicate search on 20×20px windows returns matches at r=0.98 between (527,44) and (533,290), r=0.977 between (539,164) and (599,266), r=0.974 between (593,158) and (593,260) — 250px apart and interchangeable. When I magnified those pairs, the reason they match is worse than a copy: the windows correlate because there's nothing in them *but* a mortar line. Two random pieces of this floor are the same piece of floor.

---
F1.Q6:
**YES.** It's clean, the palette holds together, the lighting falloff is handled properly, nothing is broken.

Merely competent. Not good. It clears the bar to be sold and does not clear the bar to be noticed. The layout logic is doing all the work and the material is doing none.

---
F1.Q7:
Legible at 1:1, on the face of the material: **essentially nothing.** What I can see at 1:1 is the joint grid, the crack lines, and two slabs that are a different tone from their neighbours (x 205–275 y 300–330 reads greyer; x 370–410 y 128–145 reads darker). All three of those are layout and tone, not surface. Within about one slab of the lantern — say x 430–470, y 145–170 — I can perceive that *something* is going on, a faint diagonal grain, but I cannot resolve what it is. Everywhere else the faces are flat.

Only visible under magnification: the 45° hatch stroke, the vertical tally ticks, the 1–2px dark chips scattered on faces, the dithered edge on the light mortar joints, and the fact that the west half uses a pale dotted mortar while the east half (x>440) uses a solid dark mortar — I did not see that material change at 1:1 at all, and it's the single most interesting thing on this floor.

All of that is hunting.
F1.Q7_WHY:
Checked at 1:1: the lit core x 350–500 / y 100–250; the bright northeast x 470–620 / y 30–200; the mid-left x 200–330 / y 60–200; the southwest x 200–300 / y 280–380; and both corridor mouths. Had to magnify to see anything: x 480–545 / y 55–75 (big slab interior — high-passed texture amplitude std 6.4), x 258–296 / y 110–134 (std 9.7), and x 212–254 / y 302–326 in the southwest, which measures a high-passed std of **1.24** with a total range of 9 levels on a mean luminance of 25. That slab is mathematically blank. That's the problem in one number: the surface detail is being multiplied by the light, so past roughly 100px from the lantern the texture is annihilated and the floor becomes a lit gradient with a grid ruled on it. On a phone, that's most of what's on screen.

---
F1.Q8:
Laid maybe forty years ago and walked on gently since. It reads *young*, and it reads **one single age everywhere** — I can find no part of it that is older or newer than any other part.

That is badly wrong for the fiction. This is supposed to be a floor in continuous heavy use since before the records, held by a garrison that repairs things with rope and driven pins and doesn't care how it looks. Nothing here has been repaired, replaced, worn, re-laid, or patched. There is no second generation of stone. The one thing that could have read as a repair — the odd blank grey slab at x 205–275 / y 300–330 — I magnified, and it's just a larger stone with a slightly cooler tint and a few faint vertical ticks. No fastening, no seam, no different bedding, no mismatch at its edges. It sits in the mortar exactly like its neighbours.
F1.Q8_WHY:
Slab edges are sharp everywhere — the corners at x 470/553 y 50/79, at x 415/465 y 155/185, at x 555/615 y 130/200 are all crisp right angles with no rounding, no chipping, no rocking. Mortar is intact along every joint I traced (x 185–630 at y 90, y 205, y 285); there is not one blown or missing joint in the room. Every slab sits flush — no differential settlement, no lipped edge, no slab standing proud of its neighbour. Traffic zones and non-traffic zones (compare the corridor mouth at x 376–433 y 370–395 against the dead corner at x 590–630 y 340–390) are tonally and texturally identical. The only aging signal in the entire image is the crack network, and as established in Q3 that's a decal.

---
F1.Q9:
Route: enter the west mouth at x≈185, y≈240; east along y≈240 to about x≈390; then south into the corridor at x 376–433 and off the bottom edge. Roughly an L.

**The ground told me nothing.** I routed entirely off the walls. This is the answer I'd flag hardest, because a floor in an administered underworld in four hundred years of use is the one surface that should be carrying the route — polish down the middle of the traffic line, grit and debris banked against the dead corners, the mortar worn out of the joints where feet land and intact where they don't.
F1.Q9_WHY:
Along the route: x 185–260 / y 225–260 (west approach), x 260–360 / y 225–255 (mid-crossing), x 360–433 / y 250–395 (turn and corridor mouth). Rejected: x 480–630 / y 30–200 (the northeast, dead end against the east wall at x≈630, which I confirmed is solid — no opening anywhere on it) and x 560–630 / y 300–390 (southeast corner, also dead). What's different about the ground between the walked regions and the rejected ones: **nothing.** Same joint density, same face treatment, same absence of wear. I compared the crossing at x 300 y 240 with the dead southeast corner at x 600 y 360 and the only difference is lantern falloff. If I lit them equally they'd be the same floor.

---
F1.Q10:
They all look the same. There are two openings — the west corridor mouth (x≈183, y 205–275) and the south corridor mouth (x 376–433, y 395+) — plus the room running off the top of the viewport at y=0. I magnified the ground immediately inside each mouth. The west threshold at x 185–215 / y 210–270 and the south threshold at x 376–433 / y 365–395 carry the same slab sizes, the same intact mortar, the same absence of surface wear, and no threshold stone, no scuff fan, no swept-clear centre, no banked grit at the jambs. Judged on the ground alone I cannot tell you which door the garrison uses daily and which one has been shut for a century. That information is not on this floor.

F1.CULL: Stone faces are blank at 1:1; only the joint grid and drawn-on cracks read — no material.
F1.FLIP LIST:
- Kill the repeating 45° hatch stamp and the vertical tally stamp; give slab faces per-slab variation — different stones, different tints, different wear states — so no two 20px windows are interchangeable.
- Add surface texture that survives the lighting: it currently multiplies to zero past ~100px from the lantern (measured std 1.24 at x 212–254 / y 302–326). Floor detail needs a light-independent floor, or higher base contrast, so the dim two-thirds of the room isn't a bare gradient.
- Make the cracks interact with the stone: step them at mortar joints, spall the lips, drop or lift the slabs on either side. Right now they cross joints unchanged (x 353, y 150) and read as a decal layer.
- Put age difference into the floor — at minimum one region of re-laid or replaced paving with mismatched stone, blown mortar and lipped edges, so the room has more than one generation on it. Repairs should read as the garrison's: driven pins, salvaged timber, hide, done badly.
- Wear the traffic line in: polish and worn-out mortar along the west→south crossing (y≈240, x 185–390, turning south at x 376–433), grit and debris banked in the dead northeast and southeast corners, so the ground states the route before the walls do.

F2.Q1: Cut stone paving — flat rectangular slabs, dry-ish laid with thin recessed joints. A soft, pale-tan sedimentary stone; sandstone or a soft limestone, not granite and not brick.
F2.Q1_WHY: The joint network across `(180,10)–(640,390)` resolves into discrete quadrilateral faces with darker recessed lines between them, and the courses are irregular — I measured horizontal joint spacing at roughly 21, 22, 23, 25, 27, 30, 32, 36, 37, 40, 42 px going down the room, and vertical joints breaking at unequal intervals. That's coursed rubble/ashlar paving, not tile and not a repeating brick bond. Softness comes from the damage read: the cracks are wide, branching and irregular rather than clean shear lines, and the faces chip at the joint lips (visible around `(300,300)`, `(560,290)`).
F2.Q2:
South, into the corridor at `(365–445, 390→500)`.

**Nothing about the ground influenced that.** I want to be straight about this, because I first tried to talk myself into a reason: there's a crack fan converging in the lower-centre around `(300–450, 300–390)` that appears to point at the south mouth. It doesn't — it's a coincidence of a branching pattern that runs everywhere with equal density. The ground at the south mouth `(400,385)` and the ground at the west opening `(175,215)` are the same paving, the same joint rhythm, the same crack density, the same absence of anything else. I picked south because it's the opening I could see clearly. That is a wall-geometry choice and a lighting choice, not a floor choice.
F2.Q3: It has been broken but never used. It is heavily fractured and repeatedly spattered, and it is otherwise pristine — no wear, no dirt, no rubble, no repair.
F2.Q3_WHY:
Three things I'm reading, and one absence that matters more than all three.

- A branching dark crack system, 1–2 px wide, running continuously from about `(240,60)` down through `(330,220)` and `(390,340)` and off east to `(560,300)`, with a second system through `(500,90)→(590,180)`. Each crack carries a bright 1px highlight on one side — that reads correctly as light catching a lifted lip.
- Nine or so pale rosette splashes: `(400,95)`, `(460,45)`, `(335,170)`, `(400,240)`, `(600,205)`, `(610,232)`, `(525,345)`, `(270,355)`, `(415,370)`. Template-matching one against the rest returns correlations of only 0.29–0.39, so they are genuinely varied instances, not one stamp. Good work.
- Two sunken dark panels — `(355–400, 125–142)` and `(200–290, 285–312)` — recessed, with a rounded inner outline. They read as dropped or blanked slabs.

**The absence:** there is no traffic anywhere. No polish or lightening on a walking line, no dirt or grit darkening in the joints versus mid-slab, no scuffing at either doorway threshold, no debris fallen from the cracks, no puddling in the sunken panels. And there is not one repair on this floor — no rope, no driven pin, no plank, no hide, no salvaged timber, nothing wedged or lashed. I magnified `(340,340)–(480,470)` and `(190,250)–(420,340)` specifically looking for it. It isn't there. For a floor in an administered underworld that has been in continuous heavy use since before records, held by a company that repairs everything, this floor has never been walked on and has never been fixed.
F2.Q4:
Two things.

1. **The rosettes.** They read as bright pale blooms against a dark floor and they are the highest-contrast thing on the ground. There are ~9 in `(180,10)–(640,390)` and they are *evenly distributed* — one in roughly every quadrant, none clustered, none absent. My eye hops between `(400,95)`, `(400,240)` and `(415,370)` because they sit almost on a vertical line down the room's centre, and then out to `(600,205)`/`(610,232)`, which are the only pair close together. Even scatter is the signature of a placement algorithm, not of whatever caused them.

2. **The 45° hatch.** Once I magnified `(480,20)–(660,180)` I found the same diagonal scoring motif on face after face. I template-matched one hatched face from `(520,60)` against the whole floor: matches at `(534,30)` = 0.81, `(464,127)` = 0.79, `(590,20)` = 0.74, `(582,97)` = 0.72, `(592,148)` = 0.71, `(542,19)` = 0.69, `(606,169)` = 0.68, `(604,45)` = 0.68, `(467,19)` = 0.67. Nine strong recurrences of one gesture. It is not pixel-identical — I hashed every 8/10/12/15/16/20/30 px block across the lit floor after dividing out the lighting field and found **zero** exact duplicates — but it is one stroke reused with jitter.
F2.Q5: **Made.** Zero exact block duplicates at any tested size after lighting normalisation; the courses are genuinely irregular (21–42 px); the crack network is continuous across the whole room rather than restarting at any interval; the rosettes are individually varied. There is no tiling period I can find. The caveat is Q4's hatch — the *vocabulary* is thin enough that the right-hand third feels repeated even though the pixels aren't.
F2.Q6:
**YES.**

Merely competent. Not genuinely good. The craft is real — the lighting falloff is clean, the crack highlighting is correct, the bond is irregular where a lazier floor would be gridded. But it does not do the one job the fiction gives it: it carries no information. It doesn't say who walks here, which way they go, how long they've been doing it, or that anyone has ever tried to hold the place together. It's a damage pass on a paving texture.
F2.Q7:
**Legible at 1:1 (the face, not the layout):** almost nothing. The slab faces read as soft tonal mottle — a low-amplitude noise and a broad light-to-dark gradient, and that's the whole of it. What I *can* see at 1:1 is all of it either joint or overlay: the joint lines, the black crack strokes, the pale rosettes, the two sunken panels, and the lamp falloff. Peel those off and the faces are blank.

**Only appears on magnification:** the 45° hatch scoring on essentially every face in `(480,20)–(640,180)`; rows of short vertical tick-marks reading as inscription bands at `(490–570, 25–40)` and `(490–570, 130–145)`; discrete letter-like glyph clusters at `(305,130)–(340,145)` and a single clear letterform around `(310,180)`; tally scratches at `(300,205)`; the rounded inner outline inside the sunken panel at `(360–395, 128–140)`; the fine chipping along joint lips.

That list is the problem stated plainly. There is a real second layer of authored detail on this floor — carved marks, possibly writing, in an underworld that is *a filing system for souls*, which is exactly the right idea — and at the size the game is played on a phone, none of it exists. I did not glimpse it and confirm it by zooming. I had no idea it was there until I zoomed. That is hunting, not seeing.
F2.Q8:
Centuries as a structure — but only about a week as a place. It reads as **one age everywhere**, and that single age is contradictory: the stone is old and the room is new.

The structural evidence says old: crack systems that propagate the full width of the room across dozens of slabs, two fully dropped slabs, chipped joint lips throughout. That's a century or several under load and settlement.

The surface evidence says the floor was laid yesterday: no polish on any line, no grit in any joint, no accumulation anywhere, no repair of any kind. Nothing has been *dragged* across this floor, and nobody has ever knelt on it with a hide patch and a mallet.

So I can't give you "older than the records." I can give you "old stone in a room nobody has entered." The reading that would actually match the fiction — floor laid before records, walked continuously for four hundred years, patched over and over by people who don't care how it looks — isn't on the screen.
F2.Q8_WHY: Old-stone reading from the crack runs `(240,60)→(390,340)→(560,300)` and `(500,90)→(590,180)`, the dropped panels at `(355–400,125–142)` and `(200–290,285–312)`, and the joint-lip chipping around `(300,300)` and `(560,290)`. New-room reading from the doorway approaches at `(390–440, 360–390)` and `(160–200, 190–240)`, the room's centre line `(300,180)→(500,180)`, and the joints throughout, all of which are tonally identical to untrafficked mid-slab.
F2.Q9:
Route: in at the west opening around `(175,215)`, east along `y≈200` through `(250,200)`, `(330,195)`, past the figure at `(410,180)`, then a right turn down through `(410,260)`, `(405,320)` and out the south mouth at `(405,390)`.

**The ground told me nothing.** I routed entirely off the walls. I picked `y≈200` because it's the clear span between the west mouth and the room's middle, and I turned south at `x≈405` because that's where the corridor is. If you deleted the walls and left me the floor, I could not tell you where the exits are.
F2.Q9_WHY: Along the route — `(200,205)`, `(280,200)`, `(360,195)`, `(410,240)`, `(408,300)`, `(405,375)`. Rejected — the north band `(250–500, 20–60)`, the east block `(540–630, 100–260)`, the south-west corner `(200–300, 320–385)`. **What is different about the ground between them: nothing.** Same slab sizes, same joint contrast, same crack density, same mottle amplitude, same rosette spacing. I sampled mean colour across `(230,150)–(330,250)`, `(360,250)–(460,340)`, `(540,150)–(630,250)` and `(300,15)–(420,45)`; after normalising for brightness the channel ratios sit within about 0.08 of each other, so even the apparent olive-centre/brown-edge split is the lamp, not a change in the ground. The floor is homogeneous. A route is not encoded in it.
F2.Q10: They all look the same. Judging only the ground in front of each: the west approach `(150–200, 170–260)` and the south approach `(370–440, 355–392)` carry the same paving, the same joint darkness, the same fracture density, and neither shows a fan of wear spreading from the opening, a darkened threshold, a scuffed lip, or a polished line. I magnified both specifically for this. I cannot rank them, and I cannot tell you that any of them has ever been used at all. In a place that is a filing system in continuous heavy operation, every doorway reads as never opened.
F2.CULL: No traffic wear and no repairs anywhere; surface detail is sub-legible at 1:1, so faces read blank.
F2.FLIP LIST:
- Cut a traffic path into the ground: a lighter, joint-softened band ~2 slabs wide running west mouth `(175,215)` → centre → south mouth `(405,390)`, with the joints inside it worn shallow and the joints outside it holding grit and dark.
- Differentiate the two openings — heavy fanned wear spreading from one doorway approach, and an untouched, grit-filled, undisturbed floor at the other, so the ground says which way the traffic goes before the walls do.
- Put the orcs' repairs on the floor: at least two salvaged timber planks pinned flat across the crack at `(330,220)–(390,340)`, driven pins at the joint lips near `(300,300)`, and the dropped panel at `(200–290,285–312)` bridged with lashed board — crude, oversized, unmistakable at 1:1.
- Raise the surface detail to play size: the hatch, tick-bands and glyph clusters in `(480,20)–(640,180)` and `(300,130)–(340,185)` currently vanish at 1:1. Either double their contrast and stroke weight so they read as inscription from a phone, or cut them and spend the pixels on wear.
- Break the rosette placement — nine evenly-scattered splashes at `(400,95)/(400,240)/(415,370)` etc. read as a spawn rule. Cluster them where something actually happened, leave whole quadrants clean, and vary their size by 3×.

**What to watch next:** the underlying paint is competent and the crack lighting is genuinely right — this floor's problem is not skill, it's that every mark on it is *damage* and none of it is *use*. Fix the wear and the repairs and most of the rest follows; the 1:1 legibility issue is the one that will bite twice, because it's currently costing real authored detail that nobody will ever see.
